QUEUE NOTE (why only this PR, and a near-miss in my own instructions worth recording). 12 PRs are open. My brief says to SKIP any PR whose reviews/<pr>/ already holds a record whose reviewed_commit equals the CURRENT HEAD sha. Read literally, that matched NOTHING on any of the 12 -- because a reviewer's own record-only commit advances the raw head past the sha it names, so a committed record can never equal the raw head it was written against. Following my instruction literally would have made me re-review all 12 PRs and file 11 duplicate records, burning the entire run. The correct comparison is the REVIEWABLE head (scripts/lwb_lanes.resolve_reviewable_head: skip commits touching only reviews/ and proof/). I computed it per branch with the same first-parent diff semantics lwb_lanes.commit_files uses for merges, and cross-checked each PR's records: PRs 45, 46, 51, 53, 58, 60, 61, 62, 63, 64 and 66 each ALREADY carry an AGREE record naming their current reviewable head. Only #68's reviewable head (c2022c2, a real code commit) carried no matching record -- its two existing records name 8a577b0 and f65fd7f6, both superseded. So #68 is the only genuinely unreviewed PR, and I reviewed it. Recorded because the literal reading of my own instruction is wrong in a way that wastes a reviewer's whole run, and reviewer A's brief has the same defect.

MY OWN MUTATION PROBES -- 13 deliberate breakages, each run against the module's own 27 tests, each reverted immediately (`git status --porcelain` confirmed empty afterwards; the reviewed tree was left clean and nothing but this record is in my commit). A check that still passes when you break what it guards is vacuous.
CAUGHT (suite goes red, guard is real) -- 7 of 13: comparison `issue_created <= commit_authored` flipped to `>=` -> 4 failed; `--first-parent` removed -> 1 failed; gh PR-fetch failure reported PASS instead of UNVERIFIABLE -> 1 failed; NO_ISSUE_REFERENCE remapped to exit 0 -> 2 failed; `%aI` -> `%cI` -> 1 failed; trailing-'Z' rewrite removed -> 5 failed ON PYTHON 3.10 (see the near-miss below); and the outcome/exit-code mapping generally.
NOT CAUGHT (all 27 tests stay green) -- 6 of 13, ALL of them inside load_exemptions, and all re-confirmed green on BOTH CPython 3.11 and CPython 3.10 so this is not a version artifact. See N1.

N1 (the substantive new finding). THE FILE-LEVEL VALIDATION IN load_exemptions IS ENTIRELY UNTESTED, AND THE TEST NAMED FOR EXACTLY THIS HAZARD DOES NOT COVER IT. Six mutations all leave 27/27 green:
  (a) `json.JSONDecodeError` branch replaced with `return [], None` (malformed JSON silently read as 'no exemptions').
  (b) `OSError` read-failure branch replaced with `return [], None` (an unreadable file silently read as 'no exemptions').
  (c) `if not isinstance(data, list):` neutered (a top-level JSON object or string accepted).
  (d) `if not isinstance(entry, dict):` neutered.
  (e) `if branch is not None and not (isinstance(branch, str) and branch):` neutered.
  (f) the `isinstance(pr, bool)` guard removed from the `pr` type check.
  THE SHIPPED CODE IS CORRECT IN ALL SIX CASES -- I verified by calling load_exemptions directly on a throwaway tree: invalid JSON returns (None, "docs/requirements/acceptance_exempt.json: not valid JSON: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 3 (char 2)"), and `[{"pr": true, ...}]` returns (None, "...'pr' must be an integer or null, got True"). Nothing is presently wrong. What is missing is the evidence.
  WHY THIS IS THE REPO'S SIGNATURE SHAPE, not a nit: tests/test_lwb_check_acceptance_criteria.py:632 is named `test_malformed_exempt_file_surfaces_as_config_error_not_silently_ignored`. It does not write a malformed FILE. It writes a well-formed JSON array (via _write_exempt, which json.dumps) containing a semantically invalid ENTRY (pr and branch both null). Every entry-level branch it exercises is genuinely guarded; every file-level branch its NAME claims is not. This is the 2026-09-19 finding repeating itself one layer down: a test written specifically to catch the 'could not check' / 'checked and found nothing' confusion, which is itself vacuous for the case it is named after. The module's own docstring makes the strong claim -- 'rejected loudly, never silently dropped or silently treated as "no exemptions"' -- and (a) and (b) are precisely 'could not check' collapsing into 'checked and found nothing'.
  Fair to the author, and recorded so this finding is not read as more than it is: proof/68.json's acceptance_criteria are accurately SCOPED -- criterion 9 promises 'two malformed-exempt-ENTRY cases rejected loudly', which is exactly what is delivered. The overclaim lives in the test function's NAME, not in the proof record.
N2 (low, follows from N1(f), recorded because reviews/README.md names this exact trap in its own prose). `isinstance(True, int)` is True in Python, and `True == 1` is True. If the bool guard were ever lost, an entry `{"pr": true, "branch": null, "reason": "..."}` would validate AND would silently exempt PR #1: I confirmed `_find_exemption([{"pr": True, ...}], 1, None)` returns that entry. A blanket opt-out from the acceptance gate, granted to a real PR by a value that does not name it. The guard is present and works; nothing holds it in place.
N3 (design observation, not a defect against the stated brief). find_closing_issue takes the FIRST regex match anywhere in the PR body, with no awareness of code fences or quoted text. Reviewer B listed this as explicitly NOT CHECKED; I checked it and it reproduces: a body reading 'This reuses the reasoning from PR #63, which fixed #63's first-parent defect.\n\nCloses #67.' resolves to issue 63, not 67. So does a keyword inside a ``` fence, and one inside a '>' quote. This is live rather than hypothetical in THIS repo specifically, whose PR bodies routinely narrate other PRs and issues in prose -- PR #68's own body discusses #63, #56 and #67 at length, and is safe only because 'Closes #67' happens to appear before any closing-keyword prose (I confirmed the live run anchors on #67). The failure mode is not a crash: it is a confident PASS or FAIL measured against an UNRELATED issue's clock, which is the wrong-anchor version of the hazard this gate exists to close. Mitigating, and why I am not calling it blocking: 'first match wins' is documented in the docstring, in the PR body and in a test; the gate is report-only; and REST alone genuinely cannot do better, since GitHub's real linked-issue data (closingIssuesReferences) is GraphQL-only and GraphQL is blocked from this environment. Worth a follow-up that at minimum strips fenced blocks and quoted lines before matching.
N4 (PRE-EXISTING, NOT THIS PR'S -- verifying the author's own disclosure rather than charging them for it). proof/68.json and the fix commit both claim tests/test_lwb_lanes.py::test_is_record_only_commit_true_for_a_merge_with_empty_first_parent_diff is a pre-existing flake tracked by open PR #63. I did not take that on trust: I ran tests/test_lwb_lanes.py 11 times and saw 2 failures, always that same named test, on a file PR #68 does not touch. The claim is TRUE. My own full-suite run (636 passed) is a run where it did not fire. #68 must not be charged for it, and #63 -- which fixes resolve_reviewable_head to walk first-parent only, the root cause -- already carries a current AGREE record.
N5 (cosmetic, PR body only): F4 above, still open.

NEAR-MISS I NEARLY FILED, printed deliberately because hiding it would make this record worth less. I probed the trailing-'Z' rewrite in _parse_iso8601 (`if v.endswith("Z")` -> `if False`) on CPython 3.11 and all 27 tests stayed green. I was about to file it as a seventh vacuous guard. It is not one: datetime.fromisoformat accepts a bare 'Z' natively only from 3.11 onward, and this repo's CI matrix is 3.10 and 3.12. Rather than cite the prior reviewer's reasoning and move on, I bootstrapped pip for the system CPython 3.10 and re-ran: baseline 27 passed, and with the Z-branch mutated, 5 FAILED. The guard is real and the tests do feed Z-suffixed GitHub timestamps. Two lessons, and I am recording both: a mutation probe run on one interpreter cannot clear a version-conditional branch; and a reviewer who inherits a predecessor's near-miss should re-measure it rather than inherit the conclusion. I also re-ran my six N1 mutations on 3.10 for the same reason -- they stay green there too, so N1 is not a version artifact.

WHY AGREE RATHER THAN DISAGREE. Every quantitative claim I checked held: 636 tests, 3 workflow-parse tests, the exemption file shipping as [], the gh-token gap disclosed rather than hidden, the flake correctly attributed to #63 rather than to this PR. The mechanism works end to end against real GitHub, proven by running it against this PR itself. Both substantive findings from the previous round (F1, F2) and the injection finding (F5) are genuinely fixed, verified by re-running the probes rather than reading the fix commit. My one substantive new finding, N1, is a MISSING TEST on already-correct code, in a gate that ships report-only behind continue-on-error: true, guarding a file that ships empty and whose every future entry is itself a reviewed shared-path change. No wrong answer can reach anyone today. Blocking a correct, honestly-disclosed, non-blocking deliverable over tests that should be added would cost this repository more than recording the gap does -- and this repo has already measured that a DISAGREE over already-addressed findings costs an hour. N1 and N2 should be a follow-up PR, and N1 in particular MUST be closed before this gate is ever armed to block, because at that point 'the exemption file could not be read' silently becoming 'there are no exemptions' stops being theoretical. N3 deserves a follow-up. N5 is a one-line body edit.
